newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine unions struggle to keep health monopoly.
newsitem.headline: Argentine unions struggle to keep health monopoly.

text.p: Argentina's unions are fighting to keep hold of the multibillion dollar health-plan business, which the government wants to open to competition.

The tussle is breaking out just a week after the unions organized a 36-hour general strike to protest the austere free-market policies of President Carlos Menem, who they blame for 17.1 percent unemployment.
Menem has promised to issue a decree this week to deregulate the health plans, on which the unions now have a monopolistic grip.
"We will do it in such a way that members will be able to choose between almost 300 health funds which manage $2.5 billion a year, according to their own needs," Menem said.
The unions responded by threatening a 48-hour strike.

"If the health plans are deregulated, if they begin to compete with the private funds, then pretty soon they won't even give the workers a single aspirin for their health," said the powerful truck drivers' union chief, Julio Moyano.
Raul Amin of the mechanics' union was more specific: "We are in favor of improving the health plans, but we want to keep their revenues."

But the labor leaders do not only have to face up to the government. They also have to confront the skepticism of ordinary Argentines, 80 percent of whom say they distrust unions. Only one percent of young people aged 18 to 24 say they have confidence in the unions.

Argentine law obliges all workers to pay into their union's health plan. But the poor service offered by most union plans motivates many companies also to contract private health funds for their employees, meaning a double cost.

To be sure, Menem's plan would not immediately establish free competition between the union health funds and the private funds. It would only allow workers to shift between union plans. Total competition would begin in 1998.
Menem's Cabinet Chief Jorge Rodriguez predicted that 50 of of 275 union plans would disappear by the end of the year if the government's plan was put into effect.
Private economist Aldo Abram is in favor of the government's plan. The status quo "benefits the unionists more than anyone and damages workers' interests," he said.
Private health funds, which cover three million people a year and generate revenues of $2 billion, are ecstatic at the prospect of being able to poach the unions' nine million health fund members.

But unions argue that older and poorer workers could end up without being able to pay for their health coverage. Union funds provide the same service to all their members, no matter how much they pay.

"If is deregulated...many people could end up without health cover," said economist Juan Alemann, who nonetheless is in favor of the reform as long as precautions are taken to safeguard the health of the poor.
